2.history: The river port beside the capital had barracks empty of soldiers since An Dealachadh, let by its maor to the farmers of Seann Vell for hay. When A' chiad rèisimeid was raised there in {{year:VI-0088}} from the capital's own companies the farmers were given a week to clear the long rooms, and what hay they left was fed to the regiment's horses. The regiment guards the council, the mint and the bridge over the Abhainn dhomhain, and it marched the holdouts released from the capital's gaol north to the boundary stones after the war. The town's own trade is the river: its boatmen carry the capital's goods down the Abhainn dhomhain to the sea, and since the war the regiment's stores as well, at a rate fixed by the council that the boatmen say was fixed by men who never rowed.

50.history: The walled ford town is A' chiad chabhlach's station, its hulls lying in the harbour of Doire shean a short walk away. Its ferry had carried coal across for the eastern farms every week until the fourth year, and carried grain and passengers after at a higher fare. When A' chiad chabhlach was raised in {{year:VI-0089}} from the south-west harbours, four of the ferrymen went into it, and the ferry was worked through the war by the oldest of them and his daughter. In the present year it is fitted with a dubhan engine and a chain across the ford; the old ferryman keeps his pole in the boat.
50.known_for: A' chiad chabhlach's station, and its ferry

282.history: The west-coast harbour of Cuan shean is An ceathramh cabhlach's. Its crier read the proclamation of Linn an Dubhain from the harbour steps to the fishing crews, who asked whether it changed the day of the fish-market. When An ceathramh cabhlach was raised there in {{year:VI-0090}} to join the first off the Tuathaich shore, the chandlers sold out of rope and canvas within the month. The fleet is kept on the Tuathaich coast since the war, and its watch on the Bratach Ghlas reported off the north-western cape a thing longer than the hull moving under the water.

73.history: The Tuathaich harbour facing the pirate waters kept its watch from the harbour wall with fires of the black cake from the fourth year, and its boats warned the fishing fleet in from the north-east in the year the raiders were taken off Ros dhomhain. In the war the first and fourth fleets closed Cnoc bhàn and the western Seann Skell to every boat but fishing boats, and searched those; the town shut its harbour to boats it did not know through the autumn the salt-boats were taken, and opened it again when the raiders were brought into Seann Skell. Its harbour looks north over waters the Tuathaich have fished since A' Chiad Churach, and its houses are built with their backs to the sea wind; in the war the fleets lay off the harbour mouth through the whole autumn, searching the boats that went out and again the boats that came in.
73.known_for: its watch on the pirate waters

23.history: The great city beside the old outpost is the seat of Comhairle nam Mèinnean, in the old stone house of Mac Ùisdein, and Comhairle nam Mèinnean's work in the age was done from it: its surveyors were named there for the northern inquiry, it bought An Sloc Mòr's last private share, its master Fearghas mac Aonghais called for the northern returns and had Breith Leòid read again, and Somhairle mac Lachlainn was given the western command there and chose his forty men. Ruth Calder's letter was received and filed there. An treas rèisimeid was raised under the market cross of Taigh Mhic Ùisdein in {{year:VI-0092}}. Beside that cross stands the stone set up in {{year:VI-0126}}, cut in two columns under a single heading, the regiments' dead, with the sixty-one names of Àth leathan and Muileann ghlas; Somhairle read them at its unveiling. From that year Comhairle nam Mèinnean ended the coal trade outside An Sloc Mòr. Comhairle nam Mèinnean's house keeps its northern returns, its surveys and its copy of Breith Leòid with the circuit rulings in its margins; the master of Comhairle nam Mèinnean sits in the room where Taigh Mhic Ùisdein once sat, and the house's arms are still carved above its door.
23.known_for: Comhairle nam Mèinnean's house and the stone of the sixty-one names

64.history: The walled harbour on the lake shore west of the capital raised An còigeamh rèisimeid in {{year:VI-0093}}; it mustered on the harbour wall, there being no ground inside the walls wide enough for its companies to stand in line, and was sent north to relieve the regiments before Muileann àrsaidh. The pilots of the town had asked for an engine pilot-boat in the sixth year and been told to wait for the shipwrights' guild. An còigeamh rèisimeid's barracks were raised in stone in {{year:VI-0140}}, cut by the town's quarrymen from the face that gave the harbour wall. The town's pilots have had their engine pilot-boat since the guild allowed it, and meet ships in a calm; the lake shore below the walls is An còigeamh rèisimeid's drill ground, and the town's fishermen dry their nets on the regiment's fence.
64.known_for: An còigeamh rèisimeid's walled harbour and stone barracks
